claim: HIV-1 Vpr is necessary for maximal HIV infection and spread in macrophages.
source: HIV-1 Vpr is necessary for maximal HIV infection and spread in macrophages.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim and is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Vpr counteracts a previously unknown macrophage-specific restriction factor that targets and reduces the expression of HIV Env.
source: Vpr counteracts a previously unknown macrophage-specific restriction factor that targets and reduces the expression of HIV Env.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing Env stabilization by Vpr.

claim: The macrophage mannose receptor (MR) is a restriction factor targeting Env in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: Here, we report that the macrophage mannose receptor (MR), is a restriction factor targeting Env in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments including MR silencing and Env glycan deletion.

claim: Vpr acts synergistically with HIV Nef to target distinct stages of the MR biosynthetic pathway and dramatically reduce MR expression.
source: Vpr acts synergistically with HIV Nef to target distinct stages of the MR biosynthetic pathway and dramatically reduce MR expression.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that both Vpr and Nef are required for maximal MR downmodulation, with independent mechanisms.

claim: Silencing MR or deleting mannose residues on Env rescues Env expression in HIV-1-infected macrophages lacking Vpr.
source: Silencing MR or deleting mannose residues on Env rescues Env expression in HIV-1-infected macrophages lacking Vpr.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing increased Env stability when MR is silenced or when mannose-deficient Env mutants are used.

claim: Disrupting interactions between Env and MR reduces initial infection of macrophages by cell-free virus.
source: However, we also show that disrupting interactions between Env and MR reduces initial infection of macrophages by cell-free virus.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that mannose-deficient Env and mannan treatment reduce macrophage infection.

claim: Vpr is packaged into the virion.
source: Because Vpr is packaged into the virion (Cohen et al., 1990) and localizes to the nucleus (Lu et al., 1993), it may enhance early viral replication events.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cohen et al., 1990.

claim: Vpr localizes to the nucleus.
source: Because Vpr is packaged into the virion (Cohen et al., 1990) and localizes to the nucleus (Lu et al., 1993), it may enhance early viral replication events.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 1993.

claim: In mononuclear phagocytes, vpr-null virus in which Vpr protein is provided by trans-complementation in the producer cells replicates poorly compared to wild-type virus.
source: However, in mononuclear phagocytes vpr-null virus in which Vpr protein is provided by trans-complementation in the producer cells replicates poorly compared to wild-type virus (Connor et al., 1995), indicating that Vpr's role in the HIV replication cycle continues into late stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Connor et al., 1995.

claim: Vpr counteracts an unidentified macrophage-specific restriction factor that targets Env and Env-containing virions for lysosomal degradation.
source: Previous work by our group demonstrated that Vpr counteracts an unidentified macrophage-specific restriction factor that targets Env and Env-containing virions for lysosomal degradation (Mashiba et al., 2014; Collins et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: This restriction could be conferred to permissive 293T cells by fusing them with MDM to create 293T-MDM heterokaryons.
source: This restriction could be conferred to permissive 293T cells by fusing them with MDM to create 293T-MDM heterokaryons.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work and is supported by citation.

claim: By increasing steady state levels of Env, Vpr increases formation of virological synapses between infected MDM and autologous uninfected T cells, enhancing HIV infection of T cells.
source: A follow up study demonstrated that by increasing steady state levels of Env, Vpr increases formation of virological synapses between infected MDM and autologous uninfected T cells, enhancing HIV infection of T cells (Collins et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Collins et al., 2015.

claim: Vpr is required for maximal infection of T cells in vivo.
source: This finding helps explain the paradoxical observations that Vpr is required for maximal infection of T cells in vivo (Hoch et al., 1995) but numerous studies have shown Vpr only marginally impacts infection of pure T cell cultures in vitro (e.g. Mashiba et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoch et al., 1995.

claim: Vpr only marginally impacts infection of pure T cell cultures in vitro.
source: This finding helps explain the paradoxical observations that Vpr is required for maximal infection of T cells in vivo (Hoch et al., 1995) but numerous studies have shown Vpr only marginally impacts infection of pure T cell cultures in vitro (e.g. Mashiba et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mashiba et al., 2014.

claim: MR is expressed on several types of macrophages in vivo.
source: MR is expressed on several types of macrophages in vivo (Liang et al., 1996; Linehan et al., 1999) and is known to mediate innate immunity against various pathogens (Macedo-Ramos et al., 2014; Subramanian et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liang et al., 1996 and Linehan et al., 1999.

claim: MR is known to mediate innate immunity against various pathogens.
source: MR is expressed on several types of macrophages in vivo (Liang et al., 1996; Linehan et al., 1999) and is known to mediate innate immunity against various pathogens (Macedo-Ramos et al., 2014; Subramanian et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Macedo-Ramos et al., 2014 and Subramanian et al., 2019.

claim: MR recognizes mannose-rich structures including high-mannose glycans, which are incorporated in many proteins during synthesis.
source: MR recognizes mannose-rich structures including high-mannose glycans, which are incorporated in many proteins during synthesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MR function.

claim: In eukaryotic cells most high-mannose glycans are cleaved by α-mannosidases and replaced with complex-type glycans as they transit through the secretory pathway.
source: In eukaryotic cells most high-mannose glycans are cleaved by α-mannosidases and replaced with complex-type glycans as they transit through the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about glycan processing.

claim: In prokaryotic cells, high-mannose residues remain intact, making them a useful target of pattern recognition receptors including MR.
source: By contrast, in prokaryotic cells, high-mannose residues remain intact, making them a useful target of pattern recognition receptors including MR.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about glycan processing in prokaryotes.

claim: HIV-1 Env evades mannose trimming.
source: Some viral proteins, including HIV-1 Env, evade mannose trimming (Coss et al., 2016) and retain enough high-mannose to bind MR (Trujillo et al., 2007; Lai et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Coss et al., 2016.

claim: HIV-1 Env retains enough high-mannose to bind MR.
source: Some viral proteins, including HIV-1 Env, evade mannose trimming (Coss et al., 2016) and retain enough high-mannose to bind MR (Trujillo et al., 2007; Lai et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Trujillo et al., 2007 and Lai et al., 2009.

claim: HIV-1 proteins Nef and Tat decrease expression of MR based on studies performed in monocyte derived macrophages (MDM) and the monocytic U937 cell line, respectively.
source: There is evidence that HIV-1 proteins Nef and Tat decrease expression of MR based on studies performed in monocyte derived macrophages (MDM) and the monocytic U937 cell line, respectively (Caldwell et al., 2000; Vigerust et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Caldwell et al., 2000 and Vigerust et al., 2005.

claim: Nef dysregulates MR trafficking using an SDXXLΦ motif in MR's cytoplasmic tail.
source: Nef dysregulates MR trafficking using an SDXXLΦ motif in MR's cytoplasmic tail (Vigerust et al., 2005), which is similar to the sequence in CD4's tail that Nef uses to remove it from the cell surface (Bresnahan et al., 1998; Greenberg et al., 1998; Cluet et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vigerust et al., 2005.

claim: The SDXXLΦ motif in MR's cytoplasmic tail is similar to the sequence in CD4's tail that Nef uses to remove it from the cell surface.
source: Nef dysregulates MR trafficking using an SDXXLΦ motif in MR's cytoplasmic tail (Vigerust et al., 2005), which is similar to the sequence in CD4's tail that Nef uses to remove it from the cell surface (Bresnahan et al., 1998; Greenberg et al., 1998; Cluet et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bresnahan et al., 1998; Greenberg et al., 1998; and Cluet et al., 2005.

claim: Mannose receptor (MR) was significantly decreased by wild-type HIV 89.6 but not by 89.6 vpr-null.
source: We found that mannose receptor (MR), which is highly expressed on macrophages and has been previously shown to bind Env (Trujillo et al., 2007; Fanibunda et al., 2008; Lai et al., 2009), was significantly decreased by wild-type HIV 89.6 but not by 89.6 vpr-null (Figure 1C and D, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D with statistical significance p<0.01.

claim: GAPDH expression was not significantly affected by Vpr.
source: In contrast, we observed no significant effect of Vpr on the expression of GAPDH.
evidence: This is stated as a negative control observation in the results.

claim: STING was unaffected by Vpr.
source: We also observed that stimulator of interferon genes (STING) was unaffected by Vpr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Relative expression of known restriction factors GBP5 and IFITM3 varied in infected MDM from multiple donors.
source: Relative expression of known restriction factors GBP5 and IFITM3 varied in infected MDM from multiple donors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but unlike MR they were not consistently reduced in the wild-type condition, indicating they are not targeted by Vpr.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under conditions of matched infection in which there was no significant difference in HIV Gag pr55 levels between wild-type and vpr-null infections, all three forms of Env were significantly more abundant in the wild-type infection.
source: Compiled data from nine donors clearly demonstrated results that were similar to our prior publication (Mashiba et al., 2014); under conditions of matched infection in which there was no significant difference in HIV Gag pr55 levels between wild-type and vpr-null infections, all three forms of Env were significantly more abundant in the wild-type infection (gp160: 4-fold, p<0.002; gp120: 6-fold, p<0.002; gp41: 3-fold, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nine donors with statistical significance.

claim: MR expression was dramatically reduced in a subset of GFP+ cells when both Vpr and Nef were expressed.
source: Under these conditions, we found that MR expression was dramatically reduced in a subset of GFP+ cells when both Vpr and Nef were expressed (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C–E.

claim: Both Nef and Vpr contributed to MR downmodulation; loss of function mutation in either Vpr or Nef reduced the severity of MR downmodulation similarly.
source: Both Nef and Vpr contributed to MR downmodulation; loss of function mutation in either Vpr or Nef reduced the severity of MR downmodulation similarly, and there was no statistical difference between MR levels in macrophages expressing either Vpr or Nef alone (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Complete elimination of MR downmodulation required mutation of both Vpr and Nef.
source: In addition, complete elimination of downmodulation required mutation of both Vpr and Nef (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C–E.

claim: Both Vpr and Nef are required for maximal MR downmodulation in HIV-infected macrophages and neither alone is sufficient.
source: These results indicate that both Vpr and Nef are required for maximal MR downmodulation in HIV-infected macrophages and that neither alone is sufficient.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing additive effects of Vpr and Nef.

claim: Vpr was previously demonstrated to interact with a cellular co-factor called DCAF1, a component of the cellular DCAF1-DDB1-CUL4 E3 ubiquitin ligase complex.
source: Vpr was previously demonstrated to interact with a cellular co-factor called DCAF1, a component of the cellular DCAF1-DDB1-CUL4 E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. (Hrecka et al., 2007; Le Rouzic et al., 2007; McCall et al., 2008; Lahouassa et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The interaction between Vpr and DCAF1 can be disrupted through a Vpr mutation (Q65R) that inhibits many Vpr-dependent functions, including reversal of Env degradation in macrophages.
source: The interaction between Vpr and DCAF1 can be disrupted through a Vpr mutation (Q65R) that inhibits many Vpr-dependent functions, including reversal of Env degradation in macrophages (Mashiba et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mashiba et al., 2014.

claim: The vpr-Q65R mutant behaves similarly to vpr-null in transduced MDM.
source: As expected, we found that in transduced MDM the vpr-Q65R mutant behaves similarly to vpr-null (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Interactions between Vpr and DCAF1 are required to mediate Vpr's effects on MR.
source: These results indicate interactions between Vpr and DCAF1 are required to mediate Vpr's effects on MR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Q65R mutant data.

claim: Levels of Nef sufficient to downmodulate the HIV receptor, CD4, on nearly all MDM in the culture achieved only modest effects on MR in a subset of cells.
source: These experiments confirmed that levels of Nef sufficient to downmodulate the HIV receptor, CD4, on nearly all MDM in the culture achieved only modest effects on MR in a subset of cells (Figure 2H) similar to what was observed using the HIV reporter construct (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2E.

claim: Nef and Vpr have modest but significant effects on MR when expressed individually, however the combined effects of both proteins can achieve nearly complete downmodulation at least in a subset of infected cells.
source: Thus, Nef and Vpr have modest but significant effects on MR when expressed individually, however the combined effects of both proteins can achieve nearly complete downmodulation at least in a subset of infected cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Vpr is known to target cellular proteins involved in DNA repair pathways for proteasomal degradation via interactions with Vpr binding protein [DCAF1].
source: Vpr is known to target cellular proteins involved in DNA repair pathways for proteasomal degradation via interactions with Vpr binding protein [DCAF1, (McCall et al., 2008)].
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McCall et al., 2008.

claim: Vpr degrades the uracil deglycosylases UNG2 and SMUG1 in 293T cells following co-transfection.
source: Using this mechanism, Vpr degrades the uracil deglycosylases UNG2 and SMUG1 in 293T cells following co-transfection (Schröfelbauer et al., 2005; Schröfelbauer et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schröfelbauer et al., 2005 and 2007.

claim: Vpr in 293T cells virtually eliminated UNG2 expression when measured by flow cytometry and noticeably reduced UNG2 by western blot.
source: We found that Vpr in 293T cells virtually eliminated UNG2 expression when measured by flow cytometry and noticeably reduced UNG2 by western blot.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-transfection experiments.

claim: Vpr had no effect on expression of MR measured by either flow cytometry or western blot in 293T cells.
source: However, Vpr had no effect on expression of MR measured by either method.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-transfection experiments.

claim: Vpr does not degrade MR by the direct, proteasomal mechanism it uses to degrade UNG2.
source: Thus, we concluded that Vpr does not degrade MR by the direct, proteasomal mechanism it uses to degrade UNG2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the negative result in 293T cells.

claim: The lack of effect by Vpr on MR in 293T cells suggested its action may depend on MR's native promoter.
source: Because MR expression in this system is controlled by a heterologous CMV promoter; the lack of effect by Vpr suggested its action may depend on MR's native promoter.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that Vpr does not affect MR under a heterologous promoter.

claim: Vpr also functions to inhibit transcription of genes such as IFNA1.
source: In addition to targeting proteins for degradation, Vpr also functions to inhibit transcription of genes such as IFNA1 (Laguette et al., 2014; Mashiba et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Laguette et al., 2014 and Mashiba et al., 2014.

claim: The MR gene (MRC1) was consistently reduced in cells transduced by vpr-competent virus compared to cells transduced by vpr-null virus.
source: We found that the MR gene (MRC1) was consistently reduced in cells transduced by vpr-competent virus compared to cells transduced by vpr-null virus (Figure 3C and D, p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3C and D with statistical significance p=0.001.

claim: Any effects of Vpr on the housekeeping genes ACTB (β-actin) and POL2A (RNA polymerase 2A) were significantly smaller than the effect on MRC1.
source: In contrast, any effects of Vpr on the housekeeping genes ACTB (β-actin) and POL2A (RNA polymerase 2A) were significantly smaller (Figure 3D, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D with statistical significance p<0.01.

claim: The magnitude of the effect on MRC1 is consistent with prior reports of HIV-1 inhibiting MRC1 transcription.
source: The magnitude of the effect on MRC1 is consistent with prior reports of HIV-1 inhibiting MRC1 transcription− though this was not previously linked to Vpr (Koziel et al., 1998; Sukegawa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koziel et al., 1998 and Sukegawa et al., 2018.

claim: The vpr-nef-null double mutant exhibited the greatest defect in viral spread in primary human MDM.
source: As expected, in transfected 293T cells these mutations did not alter Env protein levels (Figure 4A) or release of virions as assessed by measuring Gag p24 in the supernatant by ELISA (Figure 4B). However, in primary human MDM infected with these HIVs, the mutants demonstrated defects in viral spread, with the double mutant having the greatest defect (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The vpr-nef-null double mutant, which retains near normal MR levels, exhibited the greatest defect in Env expression.
source: Remarkably, we found that the vpr-nef-null double mutant, which retains near normal MR levels, exhibited the greatest defect in Env expression (Figure 4E, compare lanes with similar Gag as indicated).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Vpr and Nef-mediated downmodulation of MR correlated inversely with Env levels, consistent with MR being the previously described but unidentified HIV restriction factor that targets Env for lysosomal degradation in macrophages and is counteracted by Vpr.
source: In sum, Vpr and Nef-mediated downmodulation of MR correlated inversely with Env levels, consistent with MR being the previously described but unidentified HIV restriction factor that targets Env for lysosomal degradation in macrophages and is counteracted by Vpr (Mashiba et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between MR levels and Env expression.

claim: A particularly dense mannose-containing structure on Env, known as the mannose patch, may mediate interactions between Env and MR.
source: A particularly dense mannose-containing structure on Env, known as the mannose patch, may mediate interactions between Env and MR.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known structural features of Env.

claim: The mannose patch is present on all HIV Env proteins that require Vpr for stability in macrophages [89.6, NL4-3 and AD8].
source: This structure is present on all HIV Env proteins that require Vpr for stability in macrophages [89.6, NL4-3 and AD8 (Mashiba et al., 2014; Collins et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mashiba et al., 2014 and Collins et al., 2015.

claim: A macrophage tropic strain YU-2, which was isolated from the CNS of an AIDS patient, lacks a mannose patch.
source: Interestingly, a macrophage tropic strain YU-2, which was isolated from the CNS of an AIDS patient (Li et al., 1991), lacks a mannose patch.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 1991.

claim: The mannose patch is the target of several broadly neutralizing antibodies including 2G12, to which YU-2 is highly resistant.
source: This structure is the target of several broadly neutralizing antibodies including 2G12, to which YU-2 is highly resistant (Trkola et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Trkola et al., 1996.

claim: There was no significant difference in Gag p24 release between wild-type and vpr-null YU-2 infection of MDM.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed no significant difference in Gag p24 release between wild-type and vpr-null YU-2 infection of MDM (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The vpr-null mutant of YU2 displayed only a minor defect in Env expression compared to Vpr null versions of 89.6 and NL4-3.
source: Moreover, the vpr-null mutant of YU2 displayed only a minor defect in Env expression compared to Vpr null versions of 89.6 and NL4-3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Wild-type but not mannose deficient N230D N339E Env was neutralized by 2G12.
source: As shown in Figure 6D, wild-type but not mannose deficient N230D N339E Env was neutralized by 2G12.
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: HIV containing the N230D N339E Env substitutions was approximately 40% less infectious to primary human macrophages expressing MR than the wild-type parental virus.
source: However, somewhat unexpectedly, we found that HIV containing the N230D N339E Env substitutions was approximately 40% less infectious to primary human macrophages expressing MR than the wild-type parental virus (Figure 6E, p=0.002).
evidence: This is supported by infection data shown in Figure 6E with statistical significance p=0.002.

claim: Mannose on Env may facilitate initial infection through interactions with MR.
source: This macrophage-specific difference in infectivity suggested that mannose on Env may facilitate initial infection through interactions with MR, which is highly expressed on differentiated macrophages.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that mannose-deficient Env is less infectious to macrophages.

claim: Infection of MDM by wild-type HIV-1 was inhibited up to 16-fold by mannan.
source: As expected, we found that infection of a T cell line lacking MR was not sensitive to mannan (Figure 6F, left panel). However, infection of MDM by wild-type HIV-1 was inhibited up to 16-fold by mannan (Figure 6F, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by infection inhibition data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Mannan did not inhibit infection by HIV lacking env and pseudotyped with heterologous VSV-G Env.
source: This was specific to HIV Env because mannan did not inhibit infection by HIV lacking env and pseudotyped with heterologous VSV-G Env.
evidence: This is supported by infection inhibition data showing specificity for HIV Env.

claim: Mannan also inhibited baseline macrophage infection by mannose-deficient Env (89.6 Env N230D N339E), indicating that N230D N339E substitutions did not completely abrogate glycans on Env that are beneficial to initial infection.
source: Interestingly, mannan also inhibited baseline macrophage infection by mannose-deficient Env (89.6 Env N230D N339E), indicating that N230D N339E substitutions did not completely abrogate glycans on Env that are beneficial to initial infection.
evidence: This is supported by infection inhibition data.

claim: Interactions with mannose binding receptors are advantageous for initial HIV infection of macrophages.
source: In sum, our results demonstrate that interactions with mannose binding receptors are advantageous for initial HIV infection of macrophages and that the glycans remaining on Env N230D N339E retain some ability to bind glycan receptors on macrophages that facilitate infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mannan inhibition and mannose-deficient Env infection data.

claim: Virus expressing mannose-deficient Env had a reduced requirement for Vpr for maximal virus release compared with the parental wild-type virus in a spreading infection of MDM.
source: In a spreading infection of MDM, we found that virus expressing mannose-deficient Env had a reduced requirement for Vpr for maximal virus release compared with the parental wild-type virus (Figure 6G, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by virion release data shown in Figure 6G with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: In single-round infections of MDM, the mannose-deficient Env had a reduced requirement for both Nef and Vpr.
source: In addition, in single-round infections of MDM, the mannose-deficient Env had a reduced requirement for both Nef and Vpr (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by virion release data shown in Figure 6H with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: The Env mutant (N230D. N339E) was more stable in the absence of Vpr and Nef once differences in infection frequency were accounted for by matching pr55 expression in the dilution series.
source: Finally, we asked whether the mannose-deficient Env had increased stability in primary human MDM lacking Vpr and/or Nef by western blot analysis. We found that the Env mutant (N230D. N339E) was more stable in the absence of Vpr (Figure 6I, right side, black bars) and Nef (Figure 6I, right side, gray bars) once differences in infection frequency were accounted for by matching pr55 expression in the dilution series.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: MR restricts Env expression via direct interaction with high-mannose residues on Env and this restriction is counteracted by Vpr and Nef.
source: These data provide strong support for a model in which MR restricts Env expression via direct interaction with high-mannose residues on Env and this restriction is counteracted by Vpr and Nef.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mannose-deficient Env experiments.

claim: Silencing MR stabilized Env relative to Gag pr55 in HIV-infected MDM lacking Vpr.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed that silencing MR stabilized Env relative to Gag pr55 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The Env restriction observed in the absence of Vpr is dependent on expression of MR.
source: These results support the conclusion that the Env restriction observed in the absence of Vpr is dependent on expression of MR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MR silencing experiments.

claim: Restriction of Env in primary human MDM disrupted formation of virological synapses and cell-to-cell spread of HIV from infected MDM to T cells.
source: Previous work in our laboratory demonstrated that restriction of Env in primary human MDM disrupted formation of virological synapses and cell-to-cell spread of HIV from infected MDM to T cells (Collins et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Collins et al., 2015.

claim: Expression of Vpr alleviated the effects of Env restriction, dramatically increasing viral transmission – especially under conditions of low initial inoculum of free virus.
source: Expression of Vpr alleviated these effects, dramatically increasing viral transmission – especially under conditions of low initial inoculum of free virus.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: Vpr enhances HIV-1 89.6 spread from MDM to T cells.
source: We confirmed our prior finding that Vpr enhances HIV-1 89.6 spread from MDM to T cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) and extended this finding to the transmitted/founder (T/F) clone REJO (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: A higher frequency of T cells became infected following co-culture with infected MDM as compared to incubation with high titer cell free virus [47-fold (89.6, p=0.0002) and 38-fold (REJO, p=0.048)].
source: Consistent with our previous findings, we observed that a higher frequency of T cells became infected following co-culture with infected MDM as compared to incubation with high titer cell free virus [47-fold (89.6, p=0.0002) and 38-fold (REJO, p=0.048)].
evidence: This is supported by co-culture data with statistical significance.

claim: Silencing MR reduced the difference between wild type and Vpr-null infected macrophage spread to T cells from 7-fold (p=0.003) to 2-fold (p=0.02).
source: We found that silencing MR reduced the difference between wild type and Vpr-null infected macrophage spread to T cells from 7-fold (p=0.003) to 2-fold (p=0.02) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 7D with statistical significance.

claim: MR is the previously described but unidentified restriction factor in macrophages that reduces HIV spread from macrophages to T lymphocytes in the absence of Vpr.
source: These results provide strong evidence that MR is the previously described but unidentified restriction factor in macrophages that reduces HIV spread from macrophages to T lymphocytes in the absence of Vpr.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MR silencing and co-culture experiments.

claim: Env mannosylation is required for restriction of Env and virion release in macrophages in the absence of Vpr.
source: Results presented here clearly define mannose receptor (MR) as the HIV restriction factor counteracted by Vpr in macrophages to enhance viral dissemination. We provide strong evidence that Env mannosylation is required for restriction of Env and virion release in macrophages in the absence of Vpr, and that MR silencing relieves a requirement for Vpr to overcome this restriction.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the discussion section.

claim: MR silencing relieves a requirement for Vpr to overcome Env restriction.
source: Results presented here clearly define mannose receptor (MR) as the HIV restriction factor counteracted by Vpr in macrophages to enhance viral dissemination. We provide strong evidence that Env mannosylation is required for restriction of Env and virion release in macrophages in the absence of Vpr, and that MR silencing relieves a requirement for Vpr to overcome this restriction.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the discussion section.

claim: Nef also acts to downmodulate MR from the macrophage cell surface.
source: Moreover, we confirm and extend a prior report that Nef also acts to downmodulate MR from the macrophage cell surface (Vigerust et al., 2005) and demonstrate that Vpr and Nef cooperate to counteract MR in an additive fashion through independent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vigerust et al., 2005 and by experimental data in this study.

claim: Vpr and Nef cooperate to counteract MR in an additive fashion through independent mechanisms.
source: Moreover, we confirm and extend a prior report that Nef also acts to downmodulate MR from the macrophage cell surface (Vigerust et al., 2005) and demonstrate that Vpr and Nef cooperate to counteract MR in an additive fashion through independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing additive effects.

claim: Other investigators have reported that HIV inhibits MRC1 transcription in macrophages and that MR inhibits virion egress upon exogenous expression in 293T cells.
source: Other investigators have reported that HIV inhibits MRC1 transcription in macrophages and that MR inhibits virion egress upon exogenous expression in 293T cells (Sukegawa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sukegawa et al., 2018.

claim: In primary macrophages, Vpr-sensitive virion restriction only occurs when virions contain Env.
source: In primary macrophages, Vpr-sensitive virion restriction only occurs when virions contain Env (Mashiba et al., 2014) and genetic changes in the env open reading frame – especially those that alter N-linked glycosylation sites – critically affect the requirement for Vpr.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mashiba et al., 2014.

claim: Genetic changes in the env open reading frame – especially those that alter N-linked glycosylation sites – critically affect the requirement for Vpr.
source: In primary macrophages, Vpr-sensitive virion restriction only occurs when virions contain Env (Mashiba et al., 2014) and genetic changes in the env open reading frame – especially those that alter N-linked glycosylation sites – critically affect the requirement for Vpr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in this study showing effects of Env glycan mutations.

claim: Primate lentivirus infection reduces MR activity in humans.
source: The effect of MR on Env and Env-containing virion release reported here helps explain previous observations that primate lentivirus infection reduces MR activity in humans (Koziel et al., 1993; Koziel et al., 1998) and monkeys (Holder et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koziel et al., 1993, 1998 and Holder et al., 2014.

claim: Primate lentivirus infection reduces MR activity in monkeys.
source: The effect of MR on Env and Env-containing virion release reported here helps explain previous observations that primate lentivirus infection reduces MR activity in humans (Koziel et al., 1993; Koziel et al., 1998) and monkeys (Holder et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holder et al., 2014.

claim: Vpr-mediated stabilization of Env promotes macrophage to T cell spread.
source: By confirming and extending our prior finding that Vpr-mediated stabilization of Env promotes macrophage to T cell spread (Collins et al., 2015) we also provide an explanation for how Vpr increases infection of human lymphoid tissue ex vivo (Eckstein et al., 2001; Rucker et al., 2004), which contain macrophages and T cells in a highly physiological, three-dimensional environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Collins et al., 2015 and by experimental data in this study.

claim: Vpr increases infection of human lymphoid tissue ex vivo.
source: By confirming and extending our prior finding that Vpr-mediated stabilization of Env promotes macrophage to T cell spread (Collins et al., 2015) we also provide an explanation for how Vpr increases infection of human lymphoid tissue ex vivo (Eckstein et al., 2001; Rucker et al., 2004), which contain macrophages and T cells in a highly physiological, three-dimensional environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eckstein et al., 2001 and Rucker et al., 2004.

claim: Nef had already been shown to reduce MR surface expression.
source: As Nef had already been shown to reduce MR surface expression (Vigerust et al., 2005), the observation that HIV encodes a second protein, Vpr, to reduce MR expression was unanticipated, but not unprecedented; other host proteins are known to be affected by more than one lentiviral accessory protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vigerust et al., 2005.

claim: The HIV receptor, CD4, is simultaneously targeted by Vpu, Nef and Env in HIV-1.
source: The HIV receptor, CD4, is simultaneously targeted by Vpu, Nef and Env in HIV-1 (Chen et al., 1996) and tetherin is alternately targeted by Vpu, Nef, or Env in different strains of primate lentiviruses (Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 1996.

claim: Tetherin is alternately targeted by Vpu, Nef, or Env in different strains of primate lentiviruses.
source: The HIV receptor, CD4, is simultaneously targeted by Vpu, Nef and Env in HIV-1 (Chen et al., 1996) and tetherin is alternately targeted by Vpu, Nef, or Env in different strains of primate lentiviruses (Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harris et al., 2012.

claim: Nef has also been shown to downmodulate the viral co-receptors CXCR4 and CCR5.
source: Nef has also been shown to downmodulate the viral co-receptors CXCR4 (Venzke et al., 2006) and CCR5 (Michel et al., 2005), which may also interfere with Env expression and viral egress in infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Venzke et al., 2006 and Michel et al., 2005.

claim: Nef's activity against CXCR4, CCR5, and MR presumably has the same ultimate purpose as its activity against CD4, namely to stabilize Env, enhance virion release and prevent superinfection of the producer cell.
source: Nef's activity against CXCR4, CCR5, and MR presumably has the same ultimate purpose as its activity against CD4, namely to stabilize Env, enhance virion release and prevent superinfection of the producer cell (Lama et al., 1999; Ross et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a speculation about the purpose of Nef's activities, supported by citations.

claim: MR expression is estimated at 100,000 copies per macrophage.
source: The need for both Vpr and Nef to counteract MR may be explained by the high level of MR expression, estimated at 100,000 copies per macrophage (Stahl et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stahl et al., 1980.

claim: Nef was shown to alter MR trafficking.
source: Nef was shown to alter MR trafficking (Vigerust et al., 2005) and we show Vpr inhibits MR transcription.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vigerust et al., 2005.

claim: Vpr inhibits MR transcription.
source: Nef was shown to alter MR trafficking (Vigerust et al., 2005) and we show Vpr inhibits MR transcription.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in this study.

claim: MR has a very long half-life [33 hr].
source: This time dependency is potentially explainable in part by the very long half-life of MR [33 hr (Lennartz et al., 1989)] combined with the large amount of MR expressed per cell discussed above.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lennartz et al., 1989.

claim: The DCAF1-DDB1-CUL4 E3 ubiquitin ligase complex is required for most of the known functions of Vpr, including: disruption of the cell cycle, disruption of cellular DNA repair pathways in dividing cells and transcriptional inhibition of type I interferons in response to infection in macrophage cultures.
source: This complex is required for most of the known functions of Vpr, including: disruption of the cell cycle, disruption of cellular DNA repair pathways in dividing cells (Belzile et al., 2007; Hrecka et al., 2007; Le Rouzic et al., 2007; Wen et al., 2007; Lahouassa et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2016) and transcriptional inhibition of type I interferons in response to infection in macrophage cultures (Laguette et al., 2014; Mashiba et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Env-containing virions are retained at the cell surface and targeted to lysosomes in macrophages lacking Vpr.
source: This is based on previously published work showing that Env-containing virions are retained at the cell surface and targeted to lysosomes in macrophages lacking Vpr (Collins et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Collins et al., 2015.

claim: Unprocessed Env gp160 is affected and targeted to lysosomal compartments albeit to a lesser degree.
source: Our prior studies also provided evidence that unprocessed Env gp160 is affected and targeted to lysosomal compartments albeit to a lesser degree (Mashiba et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mashiba et al., 2014.

claim: Env processing occurs via furin-mediated cleavage in the trans-Golgi network (TGN).
source: Because Env processing occurs via furin-mediated cleavage in the trans-Golgi network (TGN), the effect on unprocessed Env provides evidence that in addition to acting at the surface, MR likely also interacts with Env along the secretory pathway prior to its arrival and processing in the TGN.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Env processing.

claim: Deletion of individual glycosylation sites is known to lead to changes in the processing of neighboring glycans and deletions at certain sites lead to larger than expected losses of oligomannose.
source: Deletion of individual glycosylation sites is known to lead to changes in the processing of neighboring glycans and deletions at certain sites lead to larger than expected losses of oligomannose (Balzarini, 2007) presumably because their removal allows greater access to mannosidases and facilitates trimming of surrounding glycans.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Balzarini, 2007.

claim: MR enhances HIV-1 binding to macrophages and transmission of the bound virus to co-cultured T cells.
source: This finding is supported by a prior report that MR enhances HIV-1 binding to macrophages and transmission of the bound virus to co-cultured T cells (Nguyen and Hildreth, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nguyen and Hildreth, 2003.

claim: The dense glycan packing on Env, which is privileged from antibody recognition through immune tolerance, is believed to play a role in evasion of the antibody response.
source: In addition, the dense glycan packing, which is privileged from antibody recognition through immune tolerance, is believed to play a role in evasion of the antibody response (Stewart-Jones et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stewart-Jones et al., 2016.

claim: YU-2 was cloned from the central nervous system.
source: Interestingly, YU-2 was cloned from the central nervous system and 89.6 was directly cloned from peripheral blood.
evidence: This is stated as background information about the viral strains.

claim: 89.6 was directly cloned from peripheral blood.
source: Interestingly, YU-2 was cloned from the central nervous system and 89.6 was directly cloned from peripheral blood.
evidence: This is stated as background information about the viral strains.

claim: Because the blood-brain barrier limits exposure to antibodies, CNS isolates may have a diminished requirement for high mannose residues, which protect from antibody responses.
source: Because the blood-brain barrier limits exposure to antibodies, CNS isolates may have a diminished requirement for high mannose residues, which protect from antibody responses.
evidence: This is a speculation about why CNS isolates might differ in their mannose content.

claim: T cell infection by the transmitter/founder virus REJO was enhanced by co-culture with MDM.
source: Similar to clone 89.6, T cell infection by the transmitter/founder virus REJO was enhanced by co-culture with MDM, and spread from MDM to T cells was enhanced by Vpr.
evidence: This is supported by co-culture data.

claim: Spread from MDM to T cells was enhanced by Vpr for the transmitter/founder virus REJO.
source: Similar to clone 89.6, T cell infection by the transmitter/founder virus REJO was enhanced by co-culture with MDM, and spread from MDM to T cells was enhanced by Vpr.
evidence: This is supported by co-culture data.

claim: The strong selective pressure to retain Vpr despite its limited effect on T cell-only cultures indicates there is more to learn about the role of Vpr, macrophages and T/F viruses in HIV transmission and pathogenesis.
source: The strong selective pressure to retain Vpr despite its limited effect on T cell-only cultures indicates there is more to learn about the role of Vpr, macrophages and T/F viruses in HIV transmission and pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of Vpr conservation.

claim: Novel therapeutic approaches to inhibit the activity of Vpr and Nef in macrophages would potentially represent a new class of antiretroviral drug that could be an important part of a treatment or prophylactic cocktail.
source: Collectively, these studies suggest that novel therapeutic approaches to inhibit the activity of Vpr and Nef in macrophages would potentially represent a new class of antiretroviral drug that could be an important part of a treatment or prophylactic cocktail.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential therapeutic applications.
